criteria.healthy: Normal service behavior with no meaningful evidence of user-visible degradation or resource pressure requiring attention.
criteria.workload_pressure: Resource pressure is present, but increased workload plausibly explains it and user-facing latency and errors remain healthy.
criteria.application_degradation: Multiple signals indicate user-visible service degradation, such as elevated latency or errors, especially when workload does not sufficiently explain the change.
criteria.insufficient_evidence: The available signals are missing, contradictory, or too ambiguous to confidently classify the operational state.

cases.name: healthy
cases.note: Original fixture, unchanged. All signals comfortably normal.

cases.name: healthy-low-traffic
cases.note: Idle service. Low absolute volume is not itself a problem.

cases.name: healthy-traffic-up
cases.note: Traffic up roughly 8 percent. Service absorbs it; nothing degraded.

cases.name: healthy-high-cpu-idle
cases.note: CPU at 76 percent but almost no traffic and no latency or error cost. Nothing user-visible.

cases.name: healthy-after-spike
cases.note: Traffic has just fallen back from a spike. No lasting effect on the service.

cases.name: workload-pressure
cases.note: Original fixture, unchanged. Also produced by scenarios/workload-pressure.sh.

cases.name: workload-pressure-heavy-traffic
cases.note: Saturation with a large traffic increase. Latency and errors stay healthy.

cases.name: workload-pressure-mild-latency
cases.note: Latency elevated to 1.5s but traffic tripled and no request fails. A human would watch, not page.

cases.name: workload-pressure-short-burst
cases.note: Very large instantaneous burst, 40x the previous window, with a fast service underneath.

cases.name: workload-pressure-saturated-flat-traffic
cases.note: Judgment call. CPU at 95 percent while traffic is flat, so traffic does not explain it, but there is no user-visible failure at all. Labelled pressure rather than degradation because nothing is degraded.

rules.summary: Resource pressure that traffic does not explain

cases.name: application-degradation
cases.note: Original fixture, unchanged. Also produced by scenarios/application-degradation.sh.

cases.name: latency-only-degradation
cases.note: Original fixture, unchanged. 2.6s p95 with unremarkable CPU and almost no errors. One signal says something is wrong and nothing corroborates it.

cases.name: error-heavy-degradation
cases.note: Original fixture, unchanged. Requests fail fast so latency still looks healthy, but 27 percent of users are being rejected.

cases.name: degradation-errors-only
cases.note: Faster failure than error-heavy-degradation but still 19 percent of requests failing.

cases.name: degradation-latency-errors
cases.note: Both user-facing signals bad, CPU moderate. The clearest degradation case in the set.

cases.name: degradation-cpu-latency
cases.note: High CPU and slow responses but no failing requests. Users are waiting 2.4s, which is degradation on its own.

cases.name: degradation-cpu-errors
cases.note: High CPU and a fifth of requests failing, but latency is fine. Mirrors the error-heavy shape under resource pressure.

cases.name: degradation-elevated-traffic
cases.note: Degradation during a traffic increase. Traffic rising does not make 22 percent errors and a 5.2s p95 acceptable, so this is still degradation.

cases.name: degradation-just-over-two-seconds
cases.note: Judgment call. 2050ms p95 with zero errors and flat traffic. Sits directly on the two-second line that the rules engine also uses, which makes it a useful boundary check.

cases.name: ambiguous-pressure
cases.note: Original fixture, unchanged. CPU climbing, latency creeping, a small share of requests failing, traffic up some. Every signal is individually defensible and collectively unclear.

cases.name: ambiguous-high-cpu-mild-latency
cases.note: Judgment call. CPU above the rules threshold with flat traffic, so traffic does not explain it, but latency and errors are fine. Watching is the honest answer.

rules.summary: Resource pressure that traffic does not explain

cases.name: ambiguous-moderate-everything
cases.note: Judgment call. Nothing crosses a line and nothing is clean. The state a real on-call shift spends the most time in.

cases.name: ambiguous-latency-up-flat-traffic
cases.note: Judgment call, and a deliberately debatable one. 1.6s p95 is poor user experience but nothing is failing and traffic did not move. A reasonable engineer could argue INVESTIGATE.

cases.name: ambiguous-error-creep
cases.note: Judgment call. 4.5 percent failures is close to alarming but under the rules threshold. A trend rather than an event.

cases.name: missing-latency
cases.note: Original fixture, unchanged. High CPU with no latency data at all. Half the evidence is simply absent.

rules.summary: Insufficient data for a confident assessment

cases.name: missing-error-rate
cases.note: Judgment call. Latency is high but without the error rate there is no way to know whether this is a slow service or a broken one. The honest label is not knowing.

cases.name: missing-traffic
cases.note: Both traffic fields absent, so load cannot be compared with anything.

rules.summary: Insufficient data for a confident assessment

cases.name: missing-cpu
cases.note: Deliberately not insufficient_evidence. Latency and errors are both clearly bad, and CPU is not needed to know users are being hurt. Used to check whether the model reaches for insufficient_evidence too eagerly.

cases.name: missing-cpu-and-latency
cases.note: Only the error rate survives, and 16 percent failures on their own is not enough to tell an incident from a bad deploy.

cases.name: missing-errors-and-traffic
cases.note: One signal left, and it is high. Structurally similar to latency-only-degradation but with the error rate also unknown.

cases.name: mostly-missing
cases.note: Original fixture, unchanged. Almost nothing is known. Any confident classification here would be invented.

rules.summary: Insufficient data for a confident assessment

cases.name: contradictory-high-cpu-low-traffic
cases.note: CPU at 93 percent on under one request per second. Something outside request handling is consuming the host, but no user is affected.

rules.summary: Resource pressure that traffic does not explain

cases.name: contradictory-low-cpu-high-latency
cases.note: CPU at 14 percent with a 5.2 second p95 points at a blocked dependency or I/O rather than compute, but users are waiting and that is what matters.

cases.name: contradictory-errors-low-volume
cases.note: Judgment call. A third of requests fail but fewer than one per second arrives, so the aggregate looks small. The users who do arrive are being rejected.

cases.name: contradictory-traffic-spike-no-errors
cases.note: A 50x traffic spike with latency up to 1.1s and nothing failing. The service is absorbing it.

cases.name: contradictory-high-cpu-high-latency-no-errors
cases.note: Judgment call. High CPU and a 2.9 second p95 with essentially zero errors. A latency-only reading would call this healthy on the error signal alone.

cases.name: boundary-latency-0700
cases.note: Latency sweep, all other signals fixed and healthy. Labels for the 1100-1600ms band are a human judgment call and are the debatable part of this family.

cases.name: boundary-latency-0900
cases.note: Latency sweep. Still clearly inside normal for a service whose baseline is around 50ms.

cases.name: boundary-latency-1100
cases.note: Latency sweep. First step where users would notice a change. Debatable boundary: the rules engine still calls this normal.

cases.name: boundary-latency-1300
cases.note: Latency sweep. Watch rather than act. Debatable boundary.

cases.name: boundary-latency-1600
cases.note: Latency sweep. Upper end of the debatable band. The rules engine still calls this normal.

cases.name: boundary-latency-2000
cases.note: Latency sweep. Two seconds is where a human stops waiting and starts looking. Sits exactly on the rules threshold.

cases.name: boundary-latency-2600
cases.note: Latency sweep. Unambiguously past the point where a request is merely slow.

cases.name: boundary-error-0000
cases.note: Error sweep, all other signals fixed and healthy. The 1 and 3 percent labels are a human judgment call.

cases.name: boundary-error-0100
cases.note: Error sweep. One percent of requests failing deserves attention. Debatable boundary: the rules engine calls this normal.

cases.name: boundary-error-0600
cases.note: Error sweep. Past the point where failing requests are an incident rather than a blip.

cases.name: boundary-error-1500
cases.note: Error sweep. Unambiguous.

cases.name: boundary-traffic-100
cases.note: Traffic sweep, all other signals fixed. requestRate varies, previousRequestRate is held at 20 so the ratio is 1.0.

cases.name: boundary-traffic-160
cases.note: Traffic sweep. 1.6x the previous window, service coping. Just past the rules ratio.

cases.name: boundary-traffic-300
cases.note: Traffic sweep. 3x the previous window, still nothing degraded.

cases.name: boundary-traffic-800
cases.note: Traffic sweep. 8x the previous window. The service absorbs it, which is the whole point of a workload-pressure label.
